title: Demonstrate understanding of selected texts in X

lessons.title: Reading for meaning
lessons.html:
Reading for meaning

In this unit you read different texts in your chosen language (X) and show that you understand them. At work in horticulture you read product labels, safety notices, work instructions, plant labels, memos and newsletters. In your own time you read stories, newspapers and messages.

Kinds of texts

  • Information texts: notices, instructions, labels, reports.
  • Persuasive texts: adverts, posters that want you to buy or do something.
  • Stories and poems: texts that entertain and make us think.
  • Visual texts: signs, charts, maps and pictures with few words.

Steps for reading a text

  1. Look before you read. Look at the title, headings, pictures and bold words. What is it about?
  2. Ask why it was written. To inform, to instruct, to persuade, or to entertain?
  3. Read it through once for the main idea.
  4. Read again slowly for details.
  5. Work out new words from the words around them, or ask, or use a dictionary.
  6. Sum it up in one or two sentences in your own words.

Main idea and details

The main idea is the most important point. Details support it: facts, examples, numbers, steps.

Example notice: From Monday the nursery will open at 06:30 in summer. Staff must clock in at the main gate. Please make sure the shade house doors are closed when you leave, so that the birds do not get in.

  • Main idea: new summer working arrangements at the nursery.
  • Details: opens 06:30, clock in at main gate, close shade house doors.
  • Why the doors must close: to keep birds out.

lessons.title: Understanding instructions, labels and visual texts
lessons.html:
Understanding instructions, labels and visual texts

Instructions

Instructions tell you how to do something step by step. Read all the steps before you start. Look for:

  • Numbers or words that show order: first, then, after, finally.
  • Command words: mix, water, cut, wear, do not.
  • Warnings: must, never, caution, danger.

Product labels

Fertiliser and pesticide labels contain important information. They are legal documents. Agricultural remedies are registered under Act 36 of 1947, and the label tells you how to use the product safely.

  • Name of the product and what it is for.
  • How much to use and how to mix it.
  • Safety information and the protective clothing to wear.
  • First aid instructions.
  • How to store it and get rid of the empty container.

Never guess. If you do not understand a label, ask your supervisor.

Visual texts

  • Safety signs: shape and colour give the meaning. A red circle means not allowed; a yellow triangle means warning.
  • Charts and tables: read the headings of the rows and columns first.
  • Maps and garden plans: find the key, the north arrow and the scale.

Fact or opinion?

A fact can be proved: This compost contains chicken manure. An opinion is what someone thinks: This is the best compost in South Africa. Adverts often mix facts and opinions. A careful reader can tell them apart.

Showing you understand

  • Answer questions about the text.
  • Tell someone what it says in your own words.
  • Follow the instructions correctly.
  • Say what you think of it and why.

Key points

  • Look at headings and pictures first, then read for the main idea and details.
  • Know why a text was written: to inform, instruct, persuade or entertain.
  • Read all steps of an instruction before you start.
  • Product labels are legal documents; never guess what they mean.
  • Tell facts apart from opinions.
